transcription.tex: \textbf{Pure Mathematics Year 2}\par Chapter 10: Numerical Methods\par 1. Locating roots\par 2. Using iteration to approximate roots of \(f(x)=0\)\par 3. Introduction to the Newton–Raphson method

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: At GCSE you used iteration to obtain successively better approximations to solutions. We revisit this and introduce a more powerful method.
\textbf{1. Locating roots}\par Understand what a root is and when a root must lie in an interval.\par Show that \(f(x)=x^3-4x^2+3x+1\) has a root between \(x=1.4\) and \(x=1.5\).
\textbf{2. Iteration}\par Rearrange \(f(x)=0\) as \(x=g(x)\), then use \(x_{n+1}=g(x_n)\).
\textbf{3. Newton–Raphson}\par Follow tangents to approach a root, often faster:\[x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{f(x_n)}{f^{\prime}(x_n)}.\]

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

slides.title: Why Do We Need Numerical Methods?

transcription.tex: Finding a root of \(f(x)\) means finding an input whose output is zero.
Solve \(f(x)=0\).
Some exact roots are complicated and difficult to calculate. For example, \(x^3+2x^2-3x+4=0\):
Other equations, such as \(x-\cos x=0\), have no standard exact algebraic formula for their root.
Use a numerical approximation: the root is approximately \(0.739085\).
Numerical methods give progressively better approximations to solutions of \(f(x)=0\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

slides.title: Proving a Solution Lies in an Interval

transcription.tex: Show that \(f(x)=e^x+2x-3\) has a root between \(x=0.5\) and \(x=0.6\).
If a continuous graph changes from negative to positive, its \(y\)-values must pass through zero.
\[f(0.5)=e^{0.5}+1-3=-0.351278\ldots<0,\]\[f(0.6)=e^{0.6}+1.2-3=0.022118\ldots>0.\]There is a change of sign, and \(f\) is continuous on \([0.5,0.6]\). Hence a root lies between 0.5 and 0.6.
\textbf{Exam tip}\par Calculate both endpoint values and explicitly state that there is a change of sign. Include continuity in the argument.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: A student claims: “For \(f(x)=1/x\), \(f(-1)=-1\) and \(f(1)=1\). There is a change of sign, so a root lies in \([-1,1]\).”
Why is this claim wrong?

The function is not continuous across this interval: it is undefined at \(x=0\), where there is a vertical asymptote. It never equals zero.\par A sign change guarantees a root only when the function is continuous throughout the interval. Otherwise the graph can pass from negative to positive without crossing the axis.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

slides.title: No Sign Change Does Not Mean No Root

transcription.tex: No sign change does \textbf{not} prove that an interval contains no roots.

The graph can cross the axis twice and return to the original sign. A graph can also touch the axis at a root without changing sign.\par The sign-change test can therefore miss roots: it gives a sufficient condition when continuity holds, not a necessary condition.

slides.title: Proving a Solution to a Given Accuracy

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C3 January 2013}\par \(g(x)=e^{x-1}+x-6\). Its root is \(\alpha\).\par c. By choosing a suitable interval, show that \(\alpha=2.307\) correct to 3 decimal places.\par What are the rounding boundaries?
Lower boundary: \(2.3065\).
Upper boundary: \(2.3075\).
A root strictly between these boundaries rounds to 2.307 to 3 decimal places.
\[g(2.3065)=-0.000275221\ldots<0,\]\[g(2.3075)=0.004419850\ldots>0.\]There is a change of sign, and \(g\) is continuous. Thus\[2.3065<\alpha<2.3075.\]Therefore \(\alpha=2.307\) to 3 decimal places.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: a. Sketch \(y=\ln x\) and \(y=1/x\) on the same axes. Explain why \(f(x)=\ln x-1/x\) has only one root.\par b. Show that the root lies in \(1.7<x<1.8\).\par c. Show that \(\alpha=1.763\) to 3 decimal places.
Intersections satisfy \(\ln x=1/x\), hence \(f(x)=0\). The logarithm increases and the reciprocal decreases for \(x>0\); they meet once.
\[f(1.7)=-0.057607\ldots<0,\]\[f(1.8)=0.032231\ldots>0.\]Continuity and a sign change give a root in \((1.7,1.8)\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: 2. \(f(x)=3+x^2-x^3\).\par a. Show that a root \(\alpha\) lies in \([1.8,1.9]\).\par b. Use a sign change in a suitable interval to verify \(\alpha=1.864\) to 3 decimal places.

\[f(1.8)=3+1.8^2-1.8^3\]\[=0.40800000\ldots,\]\[f(1.9)=3+1.9^2-1.9^3\]\[=-0.24900000\ldots.\]The values have opposite signs, and the function is continuous on the interval. Hence a root lies between 1.8 and 1.9.

Test the rounding boundaries:\[f(1.8635)=3+1.8635^2-1.8635^3\]\[=0.00138205\ldots,\]\[f(1.8645)=3+1.8645^2-1.8645^3\]\[=-0.00531344\ldots.\]There is a change of sign. Continuity gives \(1.8635<\alpha<1.8645\), so \(\alpha=1.864\) to 3 decimal places.

transcription.tex: 3. \(h(x)=\sqrt[3]{x}-\cos x-1\). Use radians.\par a. Show that a root \(\alpha\) lies in \([1.4,1.5]\).\par b. Use a sign change in a suitable interval to verify \(\alpha=1.441\) to 3 decimal places.

\[h(1.4)=\sqrt[3]{1.4}-\cos1.4-1\]\[=-0.05127820\ldots,\]\[h(1.5)=\sqrt[3]{1.5}-\cos1.5-1\]\[=0.07397704\ldots.\]The values have opposite signs, and the function is continuous on the interval. Hence a root lies between 1.4 and 1.5.

transcription.tex: 4. \(f(x)=\sin x-\ln x\). Use radians. The domain is \(x>0\).\par a. Show that a root \(\alpha\) lies in \([2.2,2.3]\).\par b. Use a sign change in a suitable interval to verify \(\alpha=2.219\) to 3 decimal places.

\[f(2.2)=\sin2.2-\ln2.2\]\[=0.02003904\ldots,\]\[f(2.3)=\sin2.3-\ln2.3\]\[=-0.08720391\ldots.\]The values have opposite signs, and the function is continuous on the interval. Hence a root lies between 2.2 and 2.3.

slides.title: Using Iteration to Approximate a Root

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C3 January 2013}\par \(g(x)=e^{x-1}+x-6\).\par a. Show that \(g(x)=0\) can be rearranged as \(x=\ln(6-x)+1\).\par b. Use \(x_{n+1}=\ln(6-x_n)+1\), with \(x_0=2\), to find \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) to 4 decimal places.
\textbf{Iteration rule}\par Rearrange \(f(x)=0\) into \(x=g(x)\), then use \(x_{n+1}=g(x_n)\). We will see why this works shortly.
\textbf{Tip}\par There may be several occurrences of \(x\) to isolate. Use the target equation to guide the rearrangement.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: \textbf{Edexcel C3 January 2013}\par \(g(x)=e^{x-1}+x-6\).\par a. Show that \(g(x)=0\) can be rearranged as \(x=\ln(6-x)+1\).\par b. Use \(x_{n+1}=\ln(6-x_n)+1\), with \(x_0=2\), to find \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) to 4 decimal places.
\(x_0\) is the starting value. The later terms are successive approximations to a root.
\textbf{Calculator tip}\par Enter 2 first, then enter \(\ln(6-\mathrm{Ans})+1\). Press equals repeatedly for successive iterations. Retain unrounded values during the calculation.
\textbf{Exam tip}\par Show the substitution for \(x_1\) to earn the method mark. Then state the required values of \(x_2\) and later terms.

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: The starting value matters: iteration can approach a different root, or fail to converge. Staircase and cobweb diagrams help explain why.\par \(f(x)=x^3-3x^2-2x+5\).\par a. Show there is a root in \(3<x<4\).\par b. Use \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{(x_n^3-2x_n+5)/3}\) to find \(x_1,x_2,x_3\), to 4 d.p., starting from i. \(x_0=1.5\); ii. \(x_0=4\).
\[f(3)=-1,\qquad f(4)=13.\]There is a change of sign, and \(f\) is continuous. Hence a root lies in \((3,4)\).
\[x_1=\sqrt{\frac{1.5^3-2(1.5)+5}{3}}=1.3385,\]\[x_2=1.2545,\quad x_3=1.2200.\]The changes become smaller; this sequence appears to converge to a different root.
\[x_1=4.5092,\quad x_2=5.4058,\]\[x_3=7.1219\quad\text{(4 d.p.).}\]The values grow away from the root: this iteration diverges.

Prove that the root \(\alpha=1.272\) to 3 d.p.

transcription.tex: Solve \(x^2-x-1=0\). For the positive root, rearrange as \(x=\sqrt{x+1}\) and use \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{x_n+1}\). Why does this work?
The solution of \(x=\sqrt{x+1}\) is the intersection of \(y=x\) and \(y=\sqrt{x+1}\). Its \(x\)-coordinate, \(\alpha\), is a root of the original equation.
With \(x_0=1\), find \(\sqrt{x_0+1}\): move vertically to the curve to obtain the \(y\)-value.
This gives \(x_1=\sqrt2=1.414\ldots\). Feed it back as the next input: move horizontally to \(y=x\), so the \(y\)-value becomes the new \(x\)-value.
Repeat using \(x_1=1.414\ldots\) to obtain \(x_2\), and so on.
The staircase shape gives the name: a staircase diagram. The iterates converge towards \(\alpha\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: Another rearrangement of \(x^2-x-1=0\) is \(x=1/(x-1)\). Use \(x_{n+1}=1/(x_n-1)\). What happens?
Start with a negative value, as in this diagram. Alternate between the curve \(y=1/(x-1)\) and the line \(y=x\).
The terms alternate around \(\alpha\) and move closer to it. This is a cobweb diagram. Here iteration converges to the negative root, \(\alpha=(1-\sqrt5)/2\).

sourceMapping.method: Native text and LaTeX conversion; acceptance tracked separately

transcription.tex: We can also rearrange \(x^2-x-1=0\) as \(x=x^2-1\), giving \(x_{n+1}=x_n^2-1\). What happens now?
Start to the right of the positive root. Each iteration moves farther from \(\alpha\), instead of closer. The approximations diverge, so this attempt fails.

transcription.tex: \(f(x)=x^2-8x+4\).\par a. Show that a nonnegative root can be written as \(x=\sqrt{8x-4}\).\par b. Starting with \(x_0=1\), use \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{8x_n-4}\) to draw a staircase diagram. Label \(x_0,x_1,x_2\) and the root \(\alpha\).

transcription.tex: 3. \(f(x)=x^2-6x+1\).\par a. Show that \(f(x)=0\) can be written as \(x=\sqrt{6x-1}\).\par b. Sketch \(y=x\) and \(y=\sqrt{6x-1}\).\par c. State the number of roots.
\[x^2-6x+1=0\Rightarrow x^2=6x-1.\]Both roots are positive, so take the positive square root: \(x=\sqrt{6x-1}\).
The curve meets the line twice: there are two roots.
d. Explain graphically why \(x_{n+1}=\sqrt{6x_n-1}\), \(x_0=2\), converges to a root.\par e. By sketching a diagram, explain why \(x_{n+1}=(x_n^2+1)/6\), \(x_0=10\), moves away from the roots.
Starting at 2, the staircase approaches the larger fixed point \(3+2\sqrt2\). Hence the iteration converges to this root.
Starting at 10, the steps move to larger values, farther from the fixed points. This iteration diverges.

transcription.tex: Also known as Newton’s method. We wish to find the root \(\alpha\). Start with an approximation \(x_0\), which may be well off the mark.
Follow the direction of the curve using its tangent. If the curve were reasonably straight, the point where the tangent hits the \(x\)-axis would be close to the root.
Repeat to obtain, hopefully, increasingly accurate approximations. Can you find a formula for \(x_{n+1}\) in terms of \(x_n\)?

At the tangent’s intersection with the axis, \(y=0\) and \(x=x_{n+1}\).
